recentItems.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after ‘Free Palestine’ speech | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month.
 
The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - had been the opening act for Sheeran's Loop tour, but was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches.
 
Macklemore stood by his comments on Monday, confirming that he had been cut from the tour and writing in a statement that the real victims are the Palestinian people in Gaza.
 
In his statement on Instagram, Macklemore said that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran, that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup.
 
Ed Sheeran has not yet commented, and who will replace Macklemore for the rest of the tour is unknown.

'The world needs to slow AI down' Anthropic co-founder tells BBC | BBC News
recentItems.description:
AI is getting more powerful "by the day" and a kill switch may be required by firms, one of the co-founders of AI company Anthropic has told the BBC.
 
Jack Clark says AI moves faster than other technology - "getting smarter and more capable every few months", which could become a "major risk to society".
 
During the interview with the BBC's Faisal Islam, Clark responded directly to concerns from BBC viewers - including worries about the impact on future generations.

recentItems.title: Anthropic warning: humans may need “kill switches” to shut down rogue AI systems | BBC News
recentItems.description:
AI “kill switches” may need to be mandatory for companies developing the technology, according to a co-founder of Anthropic, one of the world's largest AI firms.

Jack Clark told the BBC that a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around". Clark said "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce that.

AI's rapid developement and fears over the risks it poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms. Some have said publicly there is a chance the technology could, if unchecked, kill all humans.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored.  He said such action should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".

Jack Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI: “Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked. “ I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety. Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral.

Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was greater than 10% within the next decade. Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC he believed that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was not unreasonable.

However, some in the AI industry have also suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Fiona Bruce presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Faisal Islam and Zoe Kleinman.

recentItems.title: Is it possible to slow AI development down? | BBC Newscast
recentItems.description:
Can governments work together to regulate AI, after growing safety fears in the industry?

Donald Trump has seemingly dismissed calls for government intervention made over the weekend. The US president cited the AI race with China, saying “whoever wins AI, wins.” So is there anything the UK government can do?

Meanwhile the calls for a slow down in AI development has led to tech stocks falling in Europe, US and Asia.

Alex and James are joined by Darren Jones Labour MP and former chief secretary to the Prime Minister, who has been calling on the government for the regulation and safe development of superintelligence.
